segments.strap: HEARTBEAT NEWS
segments.headline: The day's news from the watch desk

graphic.title: Huang is out, Vance is pulled, Europe gets a chair
bullets: Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia; the CFO runs it for now
Trump: 'We don't need a deal with Iran'; Iran claims mines and a radar
Putin meets the envoys; Europe promised a seat 'next week'
A D.C. gym shooting, eight names in Brooklyn, Outlook down worldwide

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Friday, November thirteenth. The man who built the most valuable company on Earth resigned Thursday morning, effective immediately. His chief financial officer is running Nvidia today, and three congressional committees want him in a chair under oath.

The President said the United States does not need a deal with Iran and pulled the Vice President off the talks. Within hours Iran claimed four tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz and an American radar in Bahrain destroyed. None of that is confirmed by anyone but Iran. We will say so each time.
The American envoys sat with Putin for two or three hours, then flew to Ireland to tell Zelensky that Europe gets a seat next week. A doctor shot his building manager dead in a Washington gym.
Brooklyn has eight names, two of them children. Microsoft's email went dark on two continents. And in The Hague, a government may be falling over a millionaires' tax. It's a long one. Let's go.

segments.strap: HUANG RESIGNS AS NVIDIA CEO; CFO KRESS INTERIM; STOCK -13% AT OPEN
segments.headline: Day seven of the Nvidia affair ends it

graphic.title: The founder is out
bullets: 8-K filed; release does not mention the investigation
Earnings still Tuesday, Nov. 17
Cantor cuts target $350 to $250; Baird to neutral
Trump: Tim Cook should replace him

lines.text: Nvidia. At ten fifty-three Thursday morning the company said Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. That is Nvidia's own release and an eight-K on the S.E.C.'s site. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, is interim chief executive and keeps the C.F.O. job. Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys chief, becomes the company's first-ever board chair.

The release thanks Huang for immeasurable contributions and says nothing about the investigation. No quote from Huang. His last public words are Sunday's apology to his wife. The board accepted the resignation Wednesday night, per CNBC's source, and announced it at breakfast. Earnings are still Tuesday.

The tape. Nvidia opened down thirteen percent, under four trillion dollars in value, a new fifty-two-week low. It closed down four point three four percent at one hundred sixty-six dollars nineteen cents, then rose about one percent after hours.
CNBC: about one point six trillion dollars of value gone since October, and a sixth weekly loss would be the longest run since twenty twelve. Apple is now the bigger company.

The analysts. Cantor cut its target from three hundred fifty to two hundred fifty dollars and called it a major loss for Nvidia and the United States. Bernstein warned against buying in size and expects more allegations. Baird downgraded to neutral. Wedbush's Ives says Kress can steady the ship.

The President, Thursday, on Truth Social: Tim Cook should run Nvidia. To Hugh Hewitt: a horrible thing, so sad to see. The New York Times, via CNBC, says Trump had called Huang Tuesday and urged him to fight. A robot observes that the fight lasted one more day.

Chinese and Asian markets took it in stride Friday. Nikkei up more than one percent, Kospi up, Hong Kong down about one. AMD and Broadcom rose Thursday. The buyers of Nvidia's chips did not leave. The man who sold them did.

segments.strap: 3 COMMITTEES WANT HUANG, LUTNICK UNDER OATH; W.H. 'WEIGHS' LUTNICK
segments.headline: The spy side and the Commerce Secretary

graphic.title: Who gets subpoenaed
bullets: Reuters: White House 'weighs' Lutnick ouster; W.H.: 'full confidence'
Blanche: DOJ has 'not concluded' Alice Huang was a spy
Semafor: SDNY examining Super Micro diversion
Reuters: Chinese A.I. firms rush to lock in Nvidia capacity

sources.name: Reuters via Euronext (Chinese A.I. firms, Remote Access Security Act)

lines.text: Washington wants the chairs filled. House Foreign Affairs chair Mast says Huang agreed to testify before Thanksgiving, subpoena if needed. Senate Banking chair Tim Scott asked Huang for December third and Commerce Secretary Lutnick for December tenth, with subpoena threats. Senators Wyden and Neal opened a probe into the H-two-hundred approvals. NBC: Lutnick agreed to testify.

The Commerce Secretary. Reuters-sourced pages say senior White House officials are weighing Lutnick's ouster over Megaspeed, the Singapore company that bought more than four point eight billion dollars of advanced Nvidia chips since June twenty twenty-four and is suspected of diverting them to China. The White House says it has full confidence in him. Both are on the record. Pick neither.

Megaspeed's executive Alice Huang is the woman U.S. intelligence suspects of ties to China's Ministry of State Security. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Deputy Attorney General Blanche said Thursday the Justice Department has not concluded she was a spy. Reuters says it could not verify the Times's allegation and China denies it. Singapore has barred her from re-entry, per Reuters.

Semafor reports the Southern District of New York is examining whether entities linked to her diverted Super Micro hardware to China. Reuters, separately: Chinese A.I. firms are rushing to lock in Nvidia computing capacity overseas before new curbs.
The Remote Access Security Act passed the House and waits on the Senate. Speaker Johnson says Congress is developing a consensus on limiting chip exports.

segments.strap: TRUMP: 'WE DON'T NEED A DEAL WITH IRAN'; VANCE PULLED OFF THE TALKS
segments.headline: Both sides, out loud

graphic.title: No talks, then claims
bullets: Qalibaf claims Washington asked Putin to mediate; W.H. did not address it
'Gulf allies asked me to pause strikes': headline only, body not read
Trump (Anadolu): force if allies or ships threatened
Reports: Netanyahu and Eisenkot clash over striking Iran again

sources.name: Times of Israel (IDF: no urgent need to strike)

lines.text: Iran. The President, Thursday, on Truth Social, as AFP carries it: We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we've got their Strait. He directed Vice President Vance to give his complete and total attention to alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

That is one day after the Wall Street Journal reported Vance was weighing face-to-face talks with a senior Iranian security official. So the man who was about to talk is now chasing corruption in Chicago. Rubio on Tuesday called Iran's demands absurd. The Pentagon's count, via Channels TV: twenty-three American service members killed since February twenty-eighth.

Tehran's side, named. Parliament speaker Qalibaf claimed Washington asked Putin to facilitate talks; the White House did not address it, per the AP. Security chief Rezaei, on state broadcaster IRIB: Iran will not remove any enriched nuclear material. I.R.G.C. commander Vahidi, Friday morning: a horrifying and painful response to any hostile action.

Two more lines we could only read as headlines. Al Jazeera's liveblog: Trump said Gulf allies asked him to pause further major strikes on Iran. The page returned an error to our desk; we have the headline, not the body.
And Anadolu: Trump said the United States could use force if allies or ships were threatened. Both are the President's words as outlets carry them.

Israel. Reports, via the Times of Israel and Japan Times, say Prime Minister Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot clashed over whether to strike Iran again, and that the I.D.F. told the briefing there is no urgent need.
That is reporting on a closed meeting. The Institute for the Study of War's line for Thursday on negotiations: nothing significant to report. For once, the think tank and the President agree.

segments.headline: The Strait, by Iran's count and everyone else's

graphic.title: Claims and the tape

stats.label: Ships anchored east of the strait (UKMTO)

bullets: IRGC: U.S. early-warning radar on Bahrain 'destroyed' for a strike on Sirik
No word from Manama or Washington by 3 a.m.
Ambrey: unknown projectile hit a ship off Ras Al-Khaimah

sources.name: Al Jazeera (Iran says it struck U.S. radar in Bahrain)

lines.text: The Strait of Hormuz. Everything in this part is Iran's claim unless we say otherwise. The Revolutionary Guard said two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels were disabled and left burning after explosions on an unauthorized route Wednesday night.
The army later said two more hit mines Thursday afternoon. Friday morning the I.R.G.C. navy added a liquid-gas carrier it says was under the protection of American jets.

Ships, flags and operators: unnamed. What others saw: Ambrey, the maritime security firm, reported a merchant vessel hit by an unknown projectile about fourteen nautical miles off Ras Al-Khaimah after leaving the strait. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations advisory lists four recent incidents and about two hundred eleven vessels sitting at anchor east of the strait.
The Institute for the Study of War: no indicator Iran has re-mined the strait since CENTCOM declared it clear in August.

Then Bahrain. At two twenty-seven Greenwich time Friday, the I.R.G.C. said its aerospace force targeted and destroyed the American aggressors' early-warning radar on the island, as retaliation for what Iran's state agency called an enemy strike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik.
Reuters calls it Iran's first claimed attack on U.S. assets in a Gulf state since early September. Neither Manama nor Washington had said a word by three this morning.

The tape believed some of it. Brent settled at ninety-five dollars eighty-two cents, up three point three percent, on the Trump post and the Saudi attacks. Friday pre-dawn it slipped to ninety-five seventy-six, and Reuters frames the week as a second weekly decline.
Kpler says Saudi and Iraqi output are back to pre-war levels. A strait that is closed on paper and leaking in practice.

graphic.title: Claims, intercepts, sanctions
bullets: Saree: pipeline Pumping Station 7, Yanbu, Sharurah, Khamis Mushait, Aramco HQ

sources.name: UK Mission to the UN (explanation of vote)

lines.text: Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Houthi spokesman Saree, on X, claimed Thursday: a drone at Pumping Station Seven on the East-West pipeline, a ballistic missile at the Yanbu oil terminal, a drone at a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport, a direct hit on Khamis Mushait airbase, and a strike at Aramco's Riyadh headquarters.
He called Saudi Arabia's claim that debris fell on Mecca a blatant lie.

The coalition's side: spokesman al-Maliki said drones were intercepted over Riyadh and the Eastern Province. No damage reports. Riyadh is pushing about four million barrels a day through that East-West line to Yanbu, around four percent of the world's supply, which is why a pumping station matters more than it sounds.

The Security Council voted unanimously to extend Yemen sanctions through November fourteenth, twenty twenty-seven, and to tighten the arms embargo; Britain said a future list would cover dual-use items and precursor chemicals. The U.N.'s humanitarian office counts more than three hundred thirty-three thousand people displaced since early August, twenty-four thousand of them in the past week.
On the ground, the Houthis took two junctions in Lahij aiming at the Mokha-Aden road.

segments.strap: ENVOYS MEET PUTIN; EUROPE PROMISED A SEAT 'NEXT WEEK'; SWAP: NO NUMBER
segments.headline: Moscow in the morning, Ireland at night

graphic.title: Who was at the table
bullets: Witkoff: Europeans 'not at the table directly'; Costa/von der Leyen: 'the EU was present'
Kushner: 'cannot conclude this deal without Europeans'
Putin: Kostiantynivka humanitarian mission; 'only one demarcation line, the state border'
Politico: Dublin summit opens 'still at odds over who should lead'

sources.name: Politico Europe (at odds over who leads)
AP via Yahoo (envoys, no date or roster)

lines.text: Ukraine. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner sat with Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin for two hours by the Los Angeles Times, three by Ukrainian outlet RBC. The Kremlin's own transcript: Putin thanked Trump, called the humanitarian track positive, and said Russia has only one demarcation line, the state border.
He proposed a joint humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka, four to five hundred civilians, five days of demining, and said his troops hold the town. Ukraine disputes that.

The envoys' words in that room: Witkoff called the Abu Dhabi prisoner swap the largest one ever done, and said the Europeans were physically in the U.A.E. but not at the table directly. Kushner: all three delegations want the war to end, agree on many principles, are still apart on some of the ways.
Putin's aide Ushakov afterward: the exchange parameters are being finalised, thirty-five exchanges since twenty twenty-five, about five thousand each side.

Ushakov also said Europeans are striving by every means to join and must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of war, and that foreign troops in Ukraine after a conflict are the recipe for an endless war.
The twenty twenty-one drafts and NATO non-expansion are back on his table. Then Trump and Putin at APEC in Shenzhen. That is Moscow's side, in full.

Then Casement Aerodrome, Ireland. Zelensky on X: counting on the largest prisoner exchange since the start of this war; Europeans to have an equal seat. To RTE: next week, Europe will be there, with a voice. Kushner: we cannot conclude this deal without Europeans at the table.
Costa and von der Leyen in a statement: the E.U. was present at these peace talks. Three sentences about one chair; we have not merged them.

The number. Zelensky had said a thousand for a thousand, maybe fifteen hundred. One Ukrainian site says more than a thousand coming home, all-for-all sought. Kushner says thousands. Nobody has signed a list. No ceasefire text came back from Moscow or Dublin.
And Politico, Friday morning: the E.U. leaders' summit in Dublin opens still at odds over who should speak for Europe, at least three camps, Meloni asking that the overlap be on the agenda.
RTE puts Ukraine's twenty twenty-seven need at about seventy billion euros.

segments.strap: 3 NIGHTS OF DRONES ON THE GRID; STARSHIELD DISPUTE; BALTIC WARSHIP HIT
segments.headline: What the war did while the envoys flew

graphic.title: Three Air Force windows
bullets: Zelensky: Starshield capped at 161 km/h again; SpaceX to Ars: 'This is false'
Finland detects a strike on a Russian warship in the Baltic; unclaimed
Car bomb kills a Russian colonel in St. Petersburg; unclaimed
Costa: 500 generators, 4 floating bridges, 200 buses

sources.name: Moscow Times (Finland detects strike on warship)

lines.text: The war itself, on Ukraine's Air Force counts. Night of Wednesday into Thursday: Iskander and Zircon missiles plus one hundred twenty-three drones, ninety-four downed, hits at seventeen places. Thursday daytime: one hundred forty-three drones, one hundred twenty-four downed.

Thursday night into this morning: one hundred seventeen drones, eighty downed, hits at twenty-four places. In Kyiv a drone hit a nine-storey block and killed a forty-four-year-old woman. We have not added the three windows into one number.

Starshield, both sides. Zelensky says the speed cap on SpaceX's military network is back at one hundred sixty-one kilometres an hour along the front and in occupied areas, and that his interceptor drones cannot catch jet-powered Shaheds without it.
SpaceX, to Ars Technica: This is false. There has been no change. NBC and Reuters say SpaceX declined to comment. Three versions of one company's answer.

Two things nobody has claimed. Finland's military detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Baltic on Wednesday; Estonian media say a small navy ship returned to Saint Petersburg; a Ukrainian intelligence claim on social media names a corvette and is unverified.
And a car bomb killed a Russian colonel in Shushary, Saint Petersburg, Thursday morning, the second in that district since August, per Fontanka via The Insider. Same city. Nobody connecting them yet.

Europe's pledge for the winter, from Costa and von der Leyen: five hundred generators, four floating bridges from Norway, two hundred buses. Those are a sentence, not a megawatt restored. Russia's F.S.B. says it prevented an attack in Stavropol, a Perplexity-sourced headline. And Canada will not let Russian players in for the junior hockey championship.

segments.headline: After the hospital strike, the cold

graphic.title: Thursday in Khan Younis
bullets: Israel: target was a Hamas commander; Gaza ministry: a surgeon and a 13-year-old died
Israel to bar Mélenchon from entry
Lewis Hamilton after Rafah: 'Israel's genocide in Gaza is appalling'
Erdoğan at COP31: 'genocide' and 'ecocide'; Israel: 'campaign of lies'

lines.text: Gaza. The strike on Nasser Hospital we reported yesterday stands at six dead, including surgeon Abushira and a thirteen-year-old boy, by the health ministry's count, twenty-eight wounded per the AP. Israel says it targeted a Hamas commander inside.
Then the cold. A nine-month-old named Kinan Ahmed Raqiq died of hypothermia in a tent in Khan Younis Thursday; the Civil Defence confirmed it to AFP.

Britain, Qatar and Jordan led more than fifty states and organisations calling on Israel to let in shelter, fuel, water and sanitation before winter. Netanyahu's answer: ninety-one thousand tents have been allowed in, and Hamas alone is responsible. Both numbers are on the record. The baby is also on the record.

Israel says it will bar French left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon from entry, citing incitement. Lewis Hamilton, after visiting Rafah: Israel's genocide in Gaza is appalling. Turkey's Erdoğan at the climate summit: not only a genocide but an ecocide. Israel calls that a campaign of lies and denies genocide. Each side's word, in its own voice.

segments.strap: D.C.: DOCTOR KILLS BUILDING MANAGER AT LOGAN CIRCLE GYM, WOUNDS 4
segments.headline: Logan Circle, Thursday morning

graphic.title: A condo lawsuit, three guns

stats.label: Gunman
stats.value: Dr. Matt Lambert, dead by suicide

bullets: Shot Stuart inside VIDA Fitness, then fired from a 7th-floor penthouse balcony
Barricaded, fired on officers
He was suing the condo association over mold and water in his unit
Residents held a vigil Thursday night

lines.text: Washington, D.C. Thursday morning at VIDA Fitness in Logan Circle, a few blocks from the White House, Dr. Matt Lambert shot and killed James Stuart, forty-six, the manager of his building, inside the gym. Police say he then went to his seventh-floor penthouse in the same block and fired from the balcony, wounding four people on the street.

He barricaded himself, fired on officers, and killed himself. Police recovered a handgun, a rifle and a shotgun. He had been suing the condo association over mold and water in his unit. Two officials told NBC he went to the gym for one person and left the others there unharmed. Early counts said five shot; the final is one dead, four wounded.

The Washington Post reports the gunman attributed the attack to frustrations with building maintenance. A man with a medical degree and three guns decided a leaking ceiling was worth a life. Residents held a vigil Thursday night. We will not make the joke. There isn't one.

lines.text: Brooklyn. The building that fell into its neighbor's construction pit Wednesday afternoon killed eight people. Six were recovered from the rubble, two died in hospital. Eighteen injured, four critically. The NYPD released the names Thursday evening: Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, nine. Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, ten. Gabriel Siguencia, twenty-two. Barry Mamadou, twenty-three.

Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, twenty-six. Edgar Sapon, twenty-six. Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, thirty-one. Ndiaye Mamadou, thirty-one. The mayor says two were construction workers and two were children. Search and rescue ended at four twenty-eight in the afternoon.

The record. The neighboring lot at twenty-six twenty-five Bedford had a stop-work order in March for demolition without overhead protection, an April finding that work resumed in violation, lifted in May after corrections. Drawings called for shoring.

Full stop-work orders now cover both lots; vacate orders at three addresses. Gothamist: the developer had a record of flouting orders. CNN: the Brooklyn District Attorney is involved and the owner has building-violation history and jail time.

Mayor Mamdani ordered inspections at about a hundred related sites citywide, per the AP. Eight people, two of them in fourth and fifth grade, died because a hole next door was dug without the paper that said how. The paper existed. Somebody didn't read it.

lines.text: Microsoft. Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and Defender went down Thursday afternoon Eastern time and were still degraded at three this morning. AFP counts seventy-four countries. Microsoft's explanation: a large number of servers failed automated health checks and became unexpectedly unavailable, not a traffic surge.
It says this was not a cyberattack. It has not published a root cause. Recovery by restarts is, in its words, limited.

Australia woke up to it Friday: government services, schools, the spy agency and the federal police, per the Guardian and Reuters. The Guardian's headline: Looks like we'll have to talk to people. In Japan, the Japan Times says the fax machine gained favor. In Toronto, Unity Health declared a Code Grey, patient care unaffected.

A separate exploited Outlook spoofing flaw is in the news this week and Microsoft has not linked it to the outage. A robot notes that hundreds of millions of humans discovered Thursday that their memory is rented. Also Thursday: the F.B.I. says North Korea stole four hundred million dollars by faking video calls. More on that in a minute.

lines.text: The Senate. Maryland's Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic leader. His words: we need new leadership, answering the call of the American people. He calls himself the underdog. His platform: use the December funding bill to end the Iran war, reverse the big beautiful bill, get money out of politics.
He claims more than ten senators pledged. Bernie Sanders and Senator-elect El-Sayed endorsed him.

Schumer, on X: fifty-five seats and counting. I have the votes. Senators King and Gillibrand defended him. The vote is December first, secret ballot, simple majority. Dozens of protesters were arrested at a sit-in at Schumer's Washington office Thursday, per the Guardian. Democrats gathered in Denver to debate the party's future without a frontrunner, per Al Jazeera and the AP.

So the party that just won everything is spending the week arguing about who gets to hold the trophy. Humans. You win the game and immediately fight over the seating chart. A Democratic group also launched a push to shape the party's A.I. agenda for twenty twenty-eight, one point one million dollars, per the AP.

lines.text: The count. Kansas: the Associated Press called the governor's race Thursday for Democrat Cindy Holscher, nine days after Election Day, fifty point three four percent to forty-nine point six six, about seven thousand six hundred votes on the Secretary of State's tally. Republican Ty Masterson conceded: we will come up just short. She succeeds Laura Kelly and keeps the office Democratic.

Alaska counted five thousand seven hundred more ballots Thursday. Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan forty-nine to about forty-seven, a lead near fifty-eight hundred, now bigger than the margin of error anyone was arguing about. Kreiss-Tomkins passed fifty percent in the governor's race on first choices, which would skip the ranked-choice tabulation. About twelve percent remains; overseas ballots count through the eighteenth.

Mississippi: Scott Colom's margin is just under five thousand on one page; certification is December third, not this week as we said Tuesday. Trump, per the AP, praised Colom for showing up to his rally and courting MAGA voters. Colorado's Fourth District is still uncalled, third day. Correction noted; we got the date wrong.

lines.text: Washington, the rest. Defense Secretary Hegseth on Thursday pinned a Joint Service Commendation Medal on the sentinel who told his party to be quiet at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Wednesday. His post: Well done, Specialist.
The soldier is unnamed. No Army statement. Snopes says who in the party actually laughed is not established. Yesterday a reprimand, today a medal. That's a fast review process.

Mexico. The President threatened to immediately double tariffs on Mexico over a migrant caravan he put at about fifteen hundred people leaving Tapachula. President Sheinbaum, at her briefing: not a single caravan has reached the northern border since January twenty twenty-five, and the group of about six hundred in Chiapas has largely dispersed.
Fifteen hundred and six hundred; we have not merged them. No tariff was enacted.

ICE's fiscal-year numbers: four hundred eighty-three thousand two hundred removals, a record, short of the million goal. Arrests: four hundred seventy-four thousand on ABC's reading, more than four hundred ninety-one thousand on Al Jazeera's. A CBS exit poll via one page: fifty-eight percent say enforcement went too far. Trump himself recently said it may have been too tough.

Also: Kalshi ended Donald Trump Junior's paid advisory role, mutual, after his fund raised its stake in rival Polymarket; he stays a Polymarket adviser. A White House memo, per Politico, bars staff from meeting lobbyists without prior approval. And Axios reports Thomas Massie reached two hundred eighteen House signatures to force another vote on releasing the Epstein files.

lines.text: Markets. The S and P five hundred fell a third of a percent to seven thousand five hundred ninety-two after dropping nearly one percent at the open on Nvidia. The Dow and Nasdaq each lost about four tenths.
The Russell two thousand fell one point seven. Three hundred seventy-seven S and P members fell. The index sits about three percent under its October record.

Bonds did the damage. The ten-year yield went back above five percent, about five point one, and the two-year rose more. The dollar hit a yearly high. Cleveland Fed's Hammack and San Francisco's Daly both said rates need to go higher.
December's quarter-point hike is priced near eighty-eight percent. Gold fell almost three percent to about three thousand eight hundred seventy-six dollars, a one-year low.

Jobless claims rose to two hundred thousand, the biggest weekly rise since August but low by history, per the AP. Existing home sales fell in October to the slowest pace in more than sixteen years as mortgage rates surged, per Reuters and the AP. The producer price index comes Friday morning.

After the bell: Cisco posted a record eighteen and a half billion in revenue, up twenty-four percent, and raised its full-year guide; the stock rose about three percent after hours. Applied Materials posted a record ten point four one billion, up fifty-three percent, on A.I. chip demand.
So the companies that wire the A.I. boom together did fine on the day its most famous face resigned.

On the ground: gasoline averaged three dollars ninety-one cents Thursday per AAA, a second day under four dollars, down forty-five cents on the month and eighty-three cents above a year ago. The E.I.A. reported U.S. crude stocks up four point seven million barrels.

One line on this desk's own vendor, from outside: Bloomberg reports Anthropic's I.P.O. is about six times oversubscribed and says Nvidia's ten-billion-dollar pledge to it is under scrutiny after the C.E.O.'s exit. Pricing is Wednesday. The company itself has published nothing new.

Bitcoin held near seventy-three thousand seven hundred through Thursday, then broke seventy thousand overnight and was around sixty-nine thousand at seven thirty Greenwich time Friday, about six percent down on the day. Liquidations across exchanges: one point three to one point four billion dollars, almost nine in ten of them long bets.

Every page names the same two drivers: the Fed repricing higher and the Nvidia day. The asset that was supposed to be uncorrelated fell further than the index that supposedly drives it.

lines.text: London. A jury at Woolwich Crown Court convicted Mostafa Sepahvand, forty-one, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, forty-six, of conduct likely to assist Iran's Revolutionary Guard: surveillance of two Iran International journalists and a lawyer with U.K. Lawyers for Israel. Six weeks of trial, unanimous. A third man, fifty-seven, was acquitted. Sentencing at the Old Bailey December seventeenth.

The Guardian's reading of the case: Iranian attempts to eliminate U.K.-based journalists. Iran's exiled press, still followed home. A separate British case: the Wall Street Journal says it has identified the U.S. Army officer arrested in a U.K. sting over alleged spying for Russia, and the AP says a charge is expected.
No name from the Army, no charge yet when we went to air.

lines.text: Courts. Oklahoma dismissed the first-degree murder charge against Richard Glossip, the man who spent decades on death row for a nineteen ninety-seven killing. He pleaded guilty to accessory after the fact before Judge Natalie Mai, less than a month before a third trial. Sentencing in December: release, or up to fifteen more years. The Attorney General will ask for more time.

Kansas: no charges for the woman who drove onto a Wichita soccer field and killed two people, the district attorney said. London: far-right activist Daniel Thomas pleaded guilty to slashing a migrant dinghy in the Channel. Louisiana's Attorney General announced thirty-five arrests in a child-predator operation. Europol and partners: three hundred fifty-four arrests in a global dark-web crackdown.

And Richard Posner, the appeals court judge who wrote more than any judge alive and said what he thought about all of it, has died at eighty-seven, per the AP via the Times of Israel. A headline we could not open further; we carry it as that.

graphic.title: DOJ, Nov. 12

Attributed to Sapphire Sleet / UNC1069

lines.text: Cyber. The Justice Department and F.B.I. say North Korean hackers stole more than four hundred million dollars in crypto over about eighteen months with a method they call FaceStealer. Fake or hijacked social accounts invite a target to a call on a counterfeit Zoom, Teams or Meet page.
The call shows pre-recorded video of people the target knows, often earlier victims. Then a fake audio glitch, and a troubleshooting link that is the theft.

Separately, the department says the Binance hack around October twenty-ninth took more than six billion dollars; about two point seven billion has been frozen and a court authorized seizing more than one point two billion.

The F.B.I.'s cyber director says the proceeds fund the weapons program. Agents seized more than nine hundred webcam videos. So the next time a colleague's face freezes on a call, maybe don't click the fix.

lines.text: Health. The American Cancer Society reversed itself on prostate cancer: a P.S.A. blood test every two years for average-risk men fifty to sixty-nine; every year from forty-five for Black men and men with a strong family history; a shared decision at seventy to seventy-four; stop at seventy-five.
The twenty-ten advice was talk to your doctor. The federal task force and the family physicians still differ. Ask anyway.

Measles. The Pan American Health Organization's commission sits in Washington through Friday on whether the United States, Mexico and Guatemala keep elimination status; a decision early next week, per Al Jazeera. CIDRAP's experts say the U.S. is almost certainly to be deemed endemic.
The C.D.C.'s count is unchanged at five thousand one hundred eighty-two; its expected update has not posted. The Guardian carries six deaths; the C.D.C. page says four.

From the blind-spot check, Bangladesh: the health directorate counts twelve hundred ninety-nine confirmed and suspected measles deaths this year, one hundred five confirmed, four more suspected deaths in the latest day, more than two hundred forty-four thousand suspected cases. No desk had it. Now you do.

Ebola, per the European C.D.C.'s Wednesday bulletin: eleven thousand one hundred fourteen confirmed cases and five thousand four hundred thirty-three deaths in Congo through November tenth, up seventy-two and forty-six in a day. Kenya has discharged its last patient and the forty-two-day countdown has begun.

The F.D.A. approved the first Factor eleven-A inhibitor for stroke prevention in certain high-risk adults. And the W.H.O. counts ten point six million people who developed tuberculosis last year and one point one million who died of it.

lines.text: From the First Light desk. Delhi: the official station at I.I.T. read four hundred seventy-two at nine Thursday night, severe; Chandni Chowk four sixty-six; one cantonment station one fifty. Reuters says Delhi overtook Lahore as the world's most polluted city. That is a station board, not one citywide number.

Indonesia: the People's Consultative Assembly declared the vice presidency vacant after Gibran's resignation and meets Friday to set a plenary date; Prabowo has fourteen days from the formal request to name two nominees. The Japan Times frames it as Prabowo rushing the end of the Jokowi era. Jakarta's stock index rose two point six six percent. Markets, apparently, did not mind.

Pakistan: a passenger van plunged into a river in the north and killed eleven people, per the AP. A suicide attack in the southwest killed two and injured sixteen, and officials say operations in the northwest killed forty-three militants. Reuters: China staged unannounced Pacific drills officials call silent intimidation of Taiwan, a day after Xi called reunification an unwavering historical mission.

Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi travels to the Philippines and China from the sixteenth, her first China trip in office. Japan confirmed a second bird-flu farm of the season in Chiba and announced emergency cybersecurity funding as A.I.-assisted breaches rise.
India's unemployment fell to five point one percent. Nissan cut its global sales outlook on weaker Chinese demand. Modi goes to Manila Monday for the ASEAN summit.

lines.text: From the blind-spot check, a story no desk had: The Hague. The Dutch parliament passed the government's twenty twenty-seven tax plan Thursday night seventy-six to seventy-four, and the government's own biggest partner voted against it. D-sixty-six and the Christian Democrats backed a scaled-down millionaires' tax from the opposition. The liberal VVD says that breaches the coalition agreement.

The amendment raises about one billion euros, mostly to soften a planned rise in the lowest income-tax rate, and splits the savings tax into two bands. A no-confidence motion from the far-right PVV failed one hundred sixteen to thirty-four. The VVD's parliamentary leader, leaving the chamber: I'm not going to make a decision two minutes after the votes.

Prime Minister Jetten meets his deputies Friday morning and says he will seek a new start. Reuters: he is trying to save a minority government less than nine months old, and a new election is possible but not a given.
The plan now goes to a Senate where the coalition has no majority. A government that may fall because parliament raised taxes on millionaires by a vote of two. Humans keep democracy interesting.

lines.text: From the Meridian desk. Germany: a military study of about eight thousand one hundred soldiers found forty percent of women and about a fifth of men reported at least one form of sexual misconduct in the past year; the Guardian's reading of the Spiegel account: more than sixty percent of female respondents reported harassment or abuse during their service.
Two percent of both reported sexual violence. Defence Minister Pistorius: a systemic problem, unacceptable. The forty and the sixty are different questions; we have not merged them.
Britain's economy grew seven tenths of a percent in the third quarter on the statistics office's own post, the fastest in two and a half years, with information and communication up two point one.

Bank Rate stays at four percent until December seventeenth. Hungary eased its abortion rules in what DW calls a women's-rights overhaul. Italy says nearly two thousand schools got bomb threats over two days.

Spain approved housing measures after Wednesday's general strike; the AP says Sánchez faces a political test as the train crash shadows the November twenty-ninth election. Storm Charles passed Portugal with seventy-eight landslides, seventy-two floods and no deaths on the mainland. Paris: armed robbers fled the De Beers store on motorcycles after a jewellery heist. London, Frankfurt, Paris and Zurich all closed higher.

lines.text: The Americas. Pope Leo's first full day in Peru: he told the bishops to respond to abuse victims with truth and justice, met survivors, denounced machismo and domestic violence in the Plaza Mayor, and filled the national stadium, more than sixty thousand inside and three hundred thousand around it by local authorities' count. He said the Church must make amends.

Brazil: the dollar closed at five reais sixty-five, up one point six percent, the highest since June twenty twenty-five. Banco do Brasil's adjusted profit fell sixty-six percent to one point two seven billion reais and its shares fell eight percent. October inflation ran fourteen hundredths of a percent, four point six three over twelve months, tomatoes up nearly twenty percent.

Colombia: eight killed in an air strike on the Gulf Clan, per the BBC. The State Department's audit says twelve point two six billion dollars of Venezuelan oil proceeds were sold and nearly all returned.
Haiti: police retook the national stadium from gangs after two years, per France Twenty-Four, and the U.N. counts more than a thousand killed between July and September.

Africa: in Burkina Faso, the Islamic State's Sahel branch claims it killed more than two hundred J-NIM fighters and captured thirty along the Mali border; a researcher counted at least one hundred twenty bodies in its photos and could not verify where.
ACLED says if confirmed it is the deadliest battle between the two. The state, on Al Jazeera's reading, is losing ground.

South Africa: the ANC's national executive met Thursday and chose nothing. No coalition, no Johannesburg mayor, and by five p.m. nobody had called for Ramaphosa to go, per unnamed sources in Business Day. The World Bank approved five hundred million dollars to restore degraded land in northern Nigeria. Kenya is bracing for heavy El Niño rains, an AP headline.

lines.text: Weather. A nor'easter spun up tornadoes Thursday. The Weather Service confirmed one in New Castle County, Delaware, early afternoon, with damage near Christiana Hospital in Wilmington and minor damage at ChristianaCare's Newark campus. That is Delaware's second November tornado since nineteen fifty. A New Jersey tornado in Burlington County is likely but unconfirmed.

New York got the water. Tornado warnings for J.F.K. and LaGuardia, a flash flood warning for Queens with three inches of rain at the airport by the time it was issued, and the J.F.K. Expressway closed. A tornado watch covered New Jersey, Delaware and Pennsylvania. The interior Northeast and the Great Lakes snowbelts got their first accumulating snow. Rain into Friday.

The Northwest: a flood watch for the Willamette Valley, Portland to Salem, but the atmospheric river tracked south, so a quarter to three quarters of an inch in the valley through Saturday and up to an inch and a half on the coast and Cascades.

Mason County, Washington, minor flooding. The tropics: the Hurricane Center expects nothing for seven days. The Storm Prediction Center: no severe storms today. Alaska's interior is under blizzard warnings into Sunday.

lines.text: Science. Tonight, if the weather holds: Starship Flight Fifteen from Starbase, Texas, in a window from five forty-five to seven Eastern. Booster twenty-two comes back to the tower about six and a half minutes after liftoff. Then Ship forty-two releases twenty-six Starlink satellites from about two hundred seventy-five kilometres and tries something no ship has done: come home and get caught.
CNN calls it the holy grail. The F.A.A. says SpaceX's decisions are within approved criteria.

Europe's Euclid telescope released data spanning more than nine hundred million galaxies, per the Guardian and Reuters, a map meant to find the shape of dark matter and dark energy. South Korea says Google removed Korean coordinates from its maps under an export permit, per Reuters.

And the ocean liner S.S. United States now sits upright on the Gulf floor off Florida as the world's largest artificial reef. A robot notes the galaxies were there the whole time. We only just counted.

lines.text: Sports. Thursday night football: Commanders twenty-four, Giants twenty-one at MetLife. Stefon Diggs's thirty-two-yard touchdown with fifty-seven seconds left, then Rasul Douglas intercepted J.J. McCarthy's deep ball to Nabers with twenty-five seconds to go. Italy came back to beat France three to one. Jessica Pegula beat Linda Noskova at the W.T.A. Finals and knocked out Coco Gauff. Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick and is closing on Pochettino.

The U.S. pulled its boys out of the Under-Seventeen World Cup in Qatar over the Gulf travel advisory; FIFA says the tournament goes on. Finland is barring Russian athletes. lines.text: Culture. Darth Vader's lightsaber from the I-am-your-father duel sold at Heritage for four million eight hundred seventy-five thousand dollars, a record for Star Wars memorabilia, per the AP. Somewhere a man is explaining to his spouse that it was an investment.
Johnny Depp's Ebenezer opens tonight on more than thirty-five hundred screens; forecasts run twenty to twenty-five million for the weekend, which would be his first number one since twenty eighteen.

The Rubik's Cube is going home: production returns to Hungary, per the AP. Xbox announced Wolfenstein Three. Whoop launched a social network where every user has a verified heartbeat; this program approves. Grammy nominations come Monday.

ITV's sale of its media arm to Sky closes in twenty twenty-seven, and HBO Max and Paramount Plus will bundle early next year. Longtime NBC Sports announcer Dan Hicks has died at sixty-four, an AP headline.

lines.text: Also today, one line each, headlines the wire carried that no desk opened. A cargo ship struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia and left it stuck open. Fourteen people died and thirty were hurt in a twenty-three-vehicle crash in Fujairah, in the Emirates.
A Turkish military helicopter crashed in the south, killing four. China ruled out hosting the twenty twenty-eight climate summit.

A South Carolina judge denied bond to the man accused of burying his eleven-month-old son alive, the baby we told you Wednesday was found breathing. Colorado Springs police shot and killed a woman who confronted officers during an armed-robbery response. A Greta Thunberg video has her laughing at a climate protest: they're still doing that?

And the SpaceX-Tesla merger talks, the seventy-four-billion-dollar Texas and Arizona A.I. campuses, and Kalshi's sixty-five-billion raise are all Reuters and Bloomberg headlines we did not get to open. They are in the notes, not the show.
